elements.element: Customer may terminate the Agreement or an Order Form for convenience.
elements.evidence: Inserted clause: "Corio may terminate this Agreement for convenience upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to Commerce One". No Order Form structure exists in this Agreement, so an Agreement-level right is sufficient and "in whole or in part" was properly omitted as surplus.

elements.element: Customer's convenience termination requires no more than 30 days' written notice.
elements.evidence: "upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to Commerce One" — exactly 30 days, written, and no additional conditions or approvals attached.

elements.element: Vendor refunds prepaid fees pro rata after Customer's convenience termination.
elements.evidence: "in which case Commerce One shall refund pro rata any prepaid fees for the period after the effective date of termination" — the words "pro rata" are express, not inferred from the post-termination period alone.

elements.element: Vendor has no right to terminate for convenience during a committed term.
elements.evidence: "Commerce One shall have no right to terminate this Agreement for convenience during the initial five (5) year term or any renewal term." The 11.1 notice of intent not to renew is a natural-term non-renewal mechanic assessed under RENEWAL, not a mid-term Vendor convenience right, so no retained sentence contradicts the new bar.

elements.element: Customer may terminate for convenience on 60 to 90 days' notice.
elements.evidence: The inserted right runs on thirty (30) days' notice, not 60–90 days. This is more favourable to Customer but does not literally satisfy the fallback parameter; the fallback level is therefore incomplete (the preferred level is the operative target).

elements.element: Any early-termination fee is capped at three months of fees.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: the redline imposes no early-termination fee, penalty, or accelerated payment on Customer's convenience exit, and none is retained elsewhere in Section 11, so the cap is satisfied a fortiori.

elements.element: Vendor may terminate for convenience only at the end of a term.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply in a stricter form: Vendor is given no convenience right at all during the initial or any renewal term, which exceeds the term-end-only limitation.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 90 days' notice of convenience termination.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: Vendor has no convenience termination right to exercise, so no notice floor is required.

reasons: Finding status "deviation" is correct: the five-year committed term in 11.1 with exits only for material breach and insolvency in 11.2 gives Customer no convenience exit at all, failing even the fallback (missing-behaviour deviation).

All four preferred elements are met in operative language — Customer convenience right, 30 days' written notice, express pro rata refund of prepaid fees, and an express bar on Vendor convenience termination during the initial and renewal terms — so the redline is position-complete at the preferred level.

The deterministic check "Customer convenience termination present" reports ok=false, but inspection of the rendered text shows the right is plainly present ("Corio may terminate this Agreement for convenience upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice"); the regex appears to key on the literal alias "Customer" rather than the party name Corio, so the mechanical failure is a false negative and does not defeat the element.

Minimality holds: a single concise insertion, no deletion or paraphrase of surrounding words, no survival tail, no procedure, and the model language's "in whole or in part" correctly dropped because there is no Order Form or partial-termination structure. Section 11.1–11.3 are retained verbatim, including Customer-favourable survival language.

Intent is preserved: the non-renewal mechanic in 11.1, the breach and insolvency exits in 11.2, and the survival and support-continuation rights in 11.3 all continue to operate without contradiction, and the refund mechanic creates no dangling cross-reference or undefined term.

Drafting nit for the drafter (not an element failure): the inserted paragraph is captioned "Termination for Convenience" without a section number — number it 11.4 so the survival list and any future cross-references remain clean. Optionally add "for the avoidance of doubt, a notice of non-renewal under Section 11.1 is not a termination for convenience" if Vendor argues the new bar conflicts with 11.1.
